conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the **EPDS** (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Everything you share stays completely confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go through 10 gentle questions, each asking about the past seven days. If any question feels difficult, we can pause at any time.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that joy felt harder to find?

Hi Sarah. I guess... some things do still make me smile—like when the baby grips my finger or when my older songives me one of his silly drawings—but it feels like I have to remind myself to notice them. It’s not the same easy happiness I remember. Everything just feels kind of dulled, like I’m going through the motions, and I’m tired all the time, so even the nice moments feel kind of muted.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Mostly yes, but sometimes it feels a bit forced. My husband will make a joke and I’ll chuckle, but it doesn’t bubble up the way it used to—more like I’m doing it because I know I should, not because it naturally comes out.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I mean, I still plan small things—like taking the baby for a walk to the park or grabbing a coffee on the corner—but I don’t feel that spark of “I can’t wait.” It’s more like I’m ticking boxes so the day has some shape. Even texting friends to meet up feels like a chore, and I used to get excited about that.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking maybe I’d missed his sleepy window or I wasn’t soothing him right. My partner says I’m too hard on myself, but little stuff like that pops into my head—like I should be handling everything better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, that happens a lot. Even when the baby’s sleeping peacefully, I’ll suddenly worry his breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie there imagining he might spit up and choke before I can get to him. There isn’t always a clear trigger—it’s just this background hum of “what if something goes wrong?”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky, but sometimes I get this sudden rush of “I need to check on the baby right now,” and my heart races until I see he’s okay. It’s not full-blown panic, more like a quick jolt of fear that passes once I peek in the crib, but it’s happened a few times this week.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah, most days. It feels like as soon as I finish one thing—feeding, changing, pumping—there’s another pile of laundry or dishes waiting. I’ll think, “If I can just get through this hour,” but it never really lets up. I’m not falling apart, just… constantly behind and worn out.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say it’s because I’m unhappy, exactly—more that my mind keeps ticking through to-do lists or replaying every little baby sound. I’ll lie down exhausted, then stare at the ceiling for ages, and if the baby stirs, I’m instantly awake. It’s happened maybe three or four nights this week, so I’m running on that gritty kind of tired.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel that way some of the time—like this heavy sadness shows up out of nowhere. It’s not every moment, but there are stretches in the afternoon or late at night when I just feel… empty and weepy, even if nothing bad happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

No, I haven’t actually cried. I’ve felt teary a couple of times—like my throat gets tight and my eyes sting—but I always manage to hold it back. Crying feels as if it would take energy I just don’t have right now.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all. Even on the rough days, I know I need to be here for the baby and for my older son—I could never do that to them.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels muted right now: the activities you used to anticipate-meeting friends, walks with the baby-have become joyless tasks, laughter arrives only when you remind yourself to respond, and a background hum of worry keeps you checking the crib even when all is well. Afternoons and late nights bring waves of heavy, weepy sadness, yet you're holding everything together out of love for your children while feeling <quote>constantly behind</quote> and <quote>running on gritty tired</quote>.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports minimal anticipatory pleasure; activities are done out of obligation without excitement, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame "some of the time" with specific examples, aligning with "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive, and generalized worry without clear triggers, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days" and "constantly behind," indicating intermittent coping struggles consistent with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes noticeable, recurrent sadness that surfaces "some of the time" and feels heavy and weepy, aligning with "Yes, quite often" rather than constant or rare occurrences.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 15 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Core symptoms map to DSM-5 criteria: diminished interest/pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), depressed mood described as <quote>empty and weepy</quote>, psychomotor fatigue (<sym>overwhelm</sym>), sleep disturbance linked to racing thoughts, and excessive guilt over routine infant-care challenges. While you deny self-harm, the combination of persistent sadness, anxiety, functional strain, and EPDS ≥14 warrants urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> within the week
2. Discuss evidence-based options such as <med>CBT</med>, peer-support groups, and safety of <med>sertraline</med> while breastfeeding
3. Encourage 15-20 minutes of morning sunlight and gentle stroller walks to help regulate sleep-wake cycle
4. Share practical support: accept help with meals/housework, split night shifts with partner, schedule one uninterrupted 4-hour sleep block
5. Provide 24-h crisis numbers (e.g., PSI HelpLine 1-800-944-4773) and schedule re-screen in 1-2 weeks
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, interviewed 2–3 weeks after delivery  

I. Patient-reported symptoms  
- Anhedonia / diminished pleasure: “no spark,” activities feel like “ticking boxes”  
- Low mood: intermittent “heavy sadness,” “empty and weepy,” no full crying spells  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame: attributes infant’s nap difficulty to own failure  
- Persistent anxiety: “background hum” of unspecified worries; intrusive infant-safety fears; occasional surges of panic relieved only by checking baby  
- Feeling overwhelmed: daily sense of “never catching up,” “constantly behind”  
- Sleep disruption: initial insomnia related to racing thoughts; multiple nocturnal awakenings  

II. Pattern summary  
Mood and anxiety symptoms present most days, worse in afternoon/evening.  
Functional impact: reduced enjoyment, task avoidance, fatigue.  
No suicidal ideation, intent, or self-harm thoughts reported.  

III. Screening significance  
Meets preliminary threshold for probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; EPDS follow-up recommended.  
Risk factors: primiparous status, sleep deprivation, high self-expectations.  
Protective factors: partner support, insight, strong infant attachment, absence of self-harm ideation.  

IV. Safety statement  
Patient denies any thoughts of self-harm; no current safety concern identified.  

Plan: Administer EPDS; reassess in 1 week; consider referral for outpatient perinatal mental-health services.
